Quantifying the Faithfulness of Text Classification Explanations

An equal budget benchmark of SHAP, LIME and occlusion on three datasets · generated from the shapley pipeline, notebooks 01 to 07 · seed 42 · 100 reviews per dataset

Abstract

Feature attribution methods promise to show which words drive a text classifier's prediction, but different methods produce visibly different explanations, so at most one of them can be taken at face value. We compare SHAP's partition explainer, LIME, and the leave one word out occlusion baseline on three binary classification tasks: movie review sentiment (IMDB), business review sentiment (Yelp polarity) and news topic classification (AG News, business vs sci/tech), each served by an identical frozen encoder pipeline with test accuracy between 0.91 and 0.96. SHAP and LIME run at an equal budget of 500 model evaluations per explained text and again at a tenth of it; occlusion's cost is structural, one prediction per word. Faithfulness is measured by deletion: words are removed in chunks ranked by attributed importance, and the model's probability shift is recorded, in the sufficiency direction (removing unimportant text should not move the prediction) and the comprehensiveness direction (removing important text should move it), at removal thresholds of 20 to 80 percent, against each method's own shuffled control.

At the full budget, both methods outrank their randomized controls in every condition: all 108 paired control contrasts are positive, 99 of them beyond the two standard error noise threshold, the weakest at +1.2. Head to head the picture is task dependent: sufficiency favors SHAP in 6 of 27 conditions and LIME in 3, with 18 inside sampling noise; comprehensiveness favors SHAP in 4 of 27 conditions and LIME in 0, with 23 inside sampling noise. The significant differences concentrate at chunk size 1, where word level sufficiency favors SHAP on both sentiment tasks but LIME on the news topic task. Occlusion never beats a budgeted method: it loses 17 of 54 Holm corrected conditions to SHAP and 11 to LIME and wins none, so its blindness to word interactions is a measured deficit, not a theoretical one. The tenfold budget cut is survivable for SHAP, which loses ground in 9 conditions, and costly for LIME, which loses in 18; at 50 evaluations the head to head flips to SHAP outright, 7 conditions to 0. Despite near identical prediction counts, explaining all 300 reviews took 48 minutes with SHAP and 98 minutes with LIME on the same 8 core CPU, a ratio of 2.05; occlusion took 27.

1. Experimental setup

Three binary text classification datasets, one shared pipeline. Each dataset is reduced to a stratified sample of 2000 documents, split 80/20, embedded with the frozen intfloat/e5-small-v2 encoder (mean pooled, L2 normalized, 512 token limit), and classified by a single hidden layer MLP head trained on the embeddings. The classifier is deliberately simple: it exists to be explained, and keeping the pipeline constant across datasets means differences in the measurements are attributable to the data and the attribution methods rather than to modeling choices.

task train / test test accuracy explained reviews
dataset
imdb movie review sentiment 1600 / 400 0.915 100
yelp business review sentiment 1600 / 400 0.965 100
agnews news topic, business vs sci/tech 1600 / 400 0.907 100

From each test split, 100 documents are sampled with label stratification (seed 42) and explained by both methods:

  • SHAP [1], the partition explainer over a whitespace word masker, capped at 500 model evaluations per document. The cap is a budget, not an exact count: on short documents the partition tree resolves completely and stops early, which the measured prediction counts in Table 2 make visible.
  • LIME [2], ridge regression over 500 random word dropout samples per document, positional features (bow=False), dropped words replaced by the same ... marker the masker uses.
  • Occlusion [3], the leave one word out baseline: the value of a word is the drop in predicted class probability when that word alone is masked. It has no budget knob, its cost is fixed at one prediction per word plus one for the original, which places it between the two budgets on these datasets and makes it the natural fixed cost reference.

To measure how explanation power scales with budget, SHAP and LIME also run at 50 evaluations per document, a tenth of the main budget. All methods explain the predicted class and produce one signed value per whitespace word, so every downstream measurement treats them identically. Timings were recorded on the same otherwise loaded 8 core CPU machine (Intel Core Ultra 7 258V, CPU only PyTorch), so they are indicative rather than laboratory grade.

2. Related work: how explanations are evaluated, and why most metrics resist text

Doshi-Velez and Kim [4] sort interpretability evaluation into application grounded (domain experts on real tasks), human grounded (lay subjects on simplified tasks) and functionally grounded (formal proxies, no humans). Yeh et al. [5] draw the same line for feature attributions between subjective and objective measures, and observe that subjective measures have been the predominant practice. This benchmark sits deliberately on the functionally grounded, objective side, because its question, which attribution method ranks words more faithfully and at what cost, is answered by tens of thousands of scored deletions per method that no human protocol could price. The families below explain what that choice gives up and what it escapes.

Human subject metrics. The human grounded family measures what people can do with an explanation: simulate the model's output, verify a claim, reason about a counterfactual. Lage et al. [6] is the careful version of that program, and its costs are instructive: nine hundred recruited participants, two synthetic domains built so participants could bring no prior knowledge, response time, accuracy and satisfaction as outcomes, and, after all of it, no statistically significant effect of explanation variation on accuracy, their correctness signal. For text classification specifically, Nguyen [7] compared crowdsourced judgments with automatic word deletion measures and found only moderate correlation, with human judgments swayed by factors beyond the explanation itself. Human evaluation answers a question this paper does not ask, whether explanations help people, and it cannot be rerun overnight when the model, dataset or method changes.

Plausibility against human rationales. ERASER [8] scores text explanations by agreement with human annotated rationales, token F1 and intersection over union. This requires a rationale annotated corpus, which exists for a handful of datasets and must be built anew for each addition, and it measures plausibility rather than faithfulness: Jacovi and Goldberg [9] argue the two must not be conflated, since a model may genuinely rely on evidence no human would mark. Atanasova et al. [10], the closest prior diagnostic study for text classification, mix agreement with human rationales into their battery alongside faithfulness properties. Our benchmark added two datasets in one notebook without annotating a single rationale, which is the practical difference.

Infidelity, sensitivity and robustness. A third family is defined over continuous input geometry. Infidelity [5] scores an attribution by how well inner products with random perturbations predict the model's output change; robustness [11] asks that near identical inputs receive near identical attributions, formalized as local Lipschitz continuity inside an epsilon ball. Both are objective and automatic where they apply, and both presuppose operations raw text does not have: a perturbation that can be arithmetically subtracted from the input, and a neighborhood radius that means the same thing across representations. Naylor et al. [12], whose title this paper echoes, ported both metrics to clinical text through embedding space token replacement and documented where they crack: no radius transfers across text representations, and on inherently interpretable models the ground truth explanation sometimes scored worse on infidelity than post hoc surrogates, which the authors read as the metric mis transferring rather than as a fact about the explanations. Bhatt et al. [13], whose catalogue of quantitative desiderata is the broadest, formulate faithfulness as correlation over feature subsets set to a reference baseline, again a vector text lacks. Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola's own escape hatch for discrete inputs, a neighborhood over observed dataset points [11], concedes the same point.

Retraining, sanity checks and axioms. Remove and retrain, ROAR [14], deletes the top ranked features from the whole corpus and retrains the model, which controls for the distribution shift that deletion introduces but costs one full training run per method, threshold and seed, and measures a property of the dataset and training procedure as much as of the explanation. Sanity checks [15] randomize model weights and require attributions to change, and axiomatic analyses [16] certify properties such as completeness and implementation invariance; both are necessary conditions that screen out broken methods but do not rank working ones. Attention weights, the one free explanation transformers offer, are contested as explanation at all [17, 18]; Bastings and Filippova [19] argue that when the question is which input tokens mattered, saliency methods with explicit faithfulness semantics are the right tool, and this benchmark accordingly evaluates only such methods.

Where this work stands. The deletion family we build on descends from region perturbation curves for images [20] and reaches text classification as ERASER's sufficiency and comprehensiveness [8]. Its attraction is exactly what the families above lack in the text setting: deleting whole words through a masker needs no baseline vector, no epsilon ball, no arithmetic on tokens and no human annotation, and it can be recomputed for any new dataset, model or method at the price of model predictions alone. Its known weakness is that deleted text is out of distribution [14], so some output movement is guaranteed regardless of explanation quality. This benchmark's response is threefold. Every attribution source is paired with its own shuffled control, which suffers the identical distribution shift and so isolates ranking quality, the graded, comparative evaluation Jacovi and Goldberg call for [9]. Every method is scored under the same masker its attributions were computed with, at an equal, counted evaluation budget, so no method is judged against perturbation semantics it never saw or with compute another method did not get. And the per review pairing carries into the statistics, one paired test per condition on threshold averaged scores with family wise Holm correction, following standard significance testing guidance for NLP [21] and the multiple comparisons discipline of the human subject literature [6]. Zhou et al.'s survey [22] concludes that no single metric covers all aspects of interpretability, and this work does not claim otherwise: it deliberately measures neither plausibility nor human usability. The claim is narrower and checkable, that deletion faithfulness under matched budgets and matched controls is the fragment of explanation quality that is fully automatic for text classification, and that it suffices to answer which method ranks words more faithfully, and at what computational cost.

3. Faithfulness: definition

An attribution is faithful when the text it calls important is the text the model actually relies on. The measurement deletes spans and watches the output. Words are grouped into chunks of 1, 4 or 8 consecutive words, each chunk is scored from its word attributions, chunks are ranked, and the lowest or highest ranked chunks are removed by the same masker that produced the attributions, with removed spans collapsing to a ... marker. A threshold of 40 means the 40th percentile of that document's own chunk scores, so roughly 40 percent of its text is removed.

  • Sufficiency [8]: remove the least important chunks. A faithful ranking discards only noise, so the absolute probability shift should be small. Lower is better.
  • Comprehensiveness [8]: remove the most important chunks. A faithful ranking identifies what the model depends on, so the shift should be large. Higher is better.

Chunk scores combine word attributions in three ways, which disagree exactly when a chunk holds values that cancel: absolute_sum, the magnitude of the summed signed values, the theoretically motivated choice for additive attributions; sum_absolute, total magnitude regardless of direction; and max_absolute, the single strongest word.

3.1 Formal definition

Write f(s) for the model's probability of the predicted class on text s, the class fixed once from the full text. Fix a chunk size, a combination, and cut thresholds t1 < … < tn, here 20, 40, 60 and 80. For a threshold t, let s∕t− denote s with every chunk whose importance falls below the t-th percentile of s's own chunk scores removed, and s∕t+ denote s with every chunk at or above the (100−t)-th percentile removed. The two scores average the model's movement over the thresholds:

sufficiency(s) = (1/n) Σi=1…n |f(s) − f(s∕ti−)|

comprehensiveness(s) = (1/n) Σi=1…n |f(s) − f(s∕ti+)|

The relative forms divide by the model's original confidence, sufficiencyrel(s) = sufficiency(s) / f(s) and likewise for comprehensiveness, so a score reads as the share of the model's confidence the cuts moved; because the predicted class starts at or above one half, both relative scores lie in [0, 1]. Sufficiency is better when lower, comprehensiveness when higher.

A numerical example of both. Take the review of Section 5, f(s) = 0.853, explained by SHAP at the full budget, chunk size 4, absolute_sum. The four sufficiency cuts moved the model by |f(s) − f(s∕t−)| = 0.010, 0.029, 0.027, 0.037 at t = 20, 40, 60, 80; the mean is 0.026, and dividing by f(s) gives a relative sufficiency of 3.0 percent. The four comprehensiveness cuts moved it by 0.090, 0.140, 0.213, 0.196; the mean is 0.160, a relative comprehensiveness of 18.7 percent. The asymmetry between the two numbers is the faithfulness signal for this review: the words this explanation dismisses barely move the model, the words it crowns move it substantially.

Neither direction means anything in isolation, because deleted text pushes the input off the training distribution [14] and some shift is guaranteed. Every condition is therefore paired with a control in which that method's own attribution values are randomly permuted within each document, preserving the value distribution while destroying the ranking. All comparisons are paired per document: the reported advantage is the mean paired difference divided by its standard error, averaged over thresholds, so magnitudes above roughly 2 exceed sampling noise.

The budget parity is visible in the prediction counts: at each budget, SHAP and LIME made within one percent of the same number of predictions, yet LIME took roughly twice as long; occlusion's count is simply each dataset's word count plus one original per review. Two mechanisms account for the timing gap. SHAP's masker collapses each removed span into a single ... marker, so its perturbed texts shrink as the partition tree descends, while LIME keeps one marker per dropped word and its perturbed texts stay near full length for the encoder. LIME additionally pays for a ridge fit and a distance computation per document. The gap narrows on AG News, whose texts are short enough that per call overhead rather than sequence length dominates.

Two patterns stand out. First, the decisive cells sit almost entirely at chunk size 1: aggregating words into chunks of 4 or 8 washes the methods' differences into noise, consistent with the intuition that chunking averages away per word estimation error. Second, the word level winner flips with the task: SHAP's ranking is harder to beat on the two sentiment tasks, LIME's on the news topic task, where the signal concentrates in a few entity like terms that LIME's sparse linear surrogate is well shaped to isolate. Neither method dominates the grid.

4.4 One score per review: averaging over the thresholds

Averaging each review's shift over the four thresholds collapses the deletion curve into a single score per review, the area over the perturbation curve [20, 8], here on the relative scale of Section 3.1 so every number reads as percent of the model's confidence. This makes the head to head test cleaner: one paired t statistic and one Wilcoxon signed rank test per condition, on 100 paired scores, with a Holm correction across all 54 conditions. After correction, 8 conditions separate the methods: 3 favor LIME, all of them word level sufficiency on the news topic task, and 5 favor SHAP, all of them chunked comprehensiveness on Yelp. The mean level sufficiency advantages SHAP shows at the word level on the sentiment tasks (Figure 3) do not survive the rank based test, a sign they are carried by a minority of reviews with large differences rather than by a consistent per review edge.

4.5 How different are the explanations?

shap_vs_lime shap_vs_occlusion lime_vs_occlusion
dataset
imdb 0.230 0.210 0.280
yelp 0.370 0.170 0.290
agnews 0.750 0.460 0.580

Agreement between the methods tracks how concentrated the task's signal is: the median SHAP to LIME rank correlation rises from 0.23 on IMDB, where sentiment spreads across many words, to 0.75 on AG News, where a few entity terms decide the class. Even at the high end the rankings are far from identical, which makes the comparison above substantive rather than tautological: these are different explanations, not reparameterizations of one another.

4.6 Power versus the evaluation budget

How many model evaluations does a faithful explanation need? Each method appears at its two budgets, occlusion at its fixed per word cost, plotted against the predictions each source actually made. Chunk size 1 under absolute_sum is where the methods differ most and where all three combinations coincide, so it is the honest place to read budget effects. LIME at 50 samples fits its ridge surrogate on fewer samples than most documents have words, while SHAP at 50 evaluations barely splits its partition tree, so the cheap arms probe two different failure modes.

The outcome is one sided in two ways. Occlusion, despite spending more predictions than the 50 budget arms on the longer datasets, never wins a corrected condition against either full budget method: judging each word in isolation misses redundancy and interaction, and the deletion tests price that blindness directly. And the budgets are not symmetric between methods. LIME loses 18 of 54 conditions to its own full budget arm, twice SHAP's 9, because a ridge surrogate fitted on 50 dropout samples is underdetermined for documents with more words than samples, while SHAP's partition estimates merely get coarser. At the cheap budget the head to head accordingly flips to SHAP outright, 7 conditions to 0.

5. Worked example: the same review under all three methods

One IMDB review, predicted positive with probability 0.853, explained by all three methods from the benchmark caches. The SHAP to LIME Spearman rank correlation on this review is 0.69.

6. Conclusion

Under an equal evaluation budget, both SHAP and LIME rank text more faithfully than chance in every condition tested: all 108 paired contrasts against shuffled controls are positive and 99 exceed the noise threshold, with the weakest at +1.2 standard errors. Head to head, sufficiency favors SHAP in 6 of 27 conditions and LIME in 3, with 18 inside sampling noise, and comprehensiveness favors SHAP in 4 of 27 conditions and LIME in 0, with 23 inside sampling noise. The decisive cells concentrate at the word level and flip with the task, SHAP ahead on both sentiment datasets, LIME ahead on the news topic dataset, while chunked conditions are almost uniformly within noise. The threshold averaged scores sharpen this further: after Holm correction only 8 of 54 comparisons separate the methods, 3 for LIME (word level sufficiency on the topic task) and 5 for SHAP (chunked comprehensiveness on Yelp). Neither method dominates.

The budget arm turns those observations into practical guidance. Cutting the budget tenfold never helps: the full budget wins 9 of 54 Holm corrected conditions for SHAP and 18 for LIME, the cheap arms none, and at 50 evaluations the method comparison flips decisively to SHAP (7 conditions to 0). Occlusion, whose cost is one prediction per word, never wins a corrected condition against either full budget method, losing 17 to SHAP and 11 to LIME (Tables 8 and 9, Figure 4). When evaluations are scarce, these results say to spend them on SHAP; and occlusion's simplicity buys strictly less faithfulness than the same predictions spent on either budgeted method.

The practical reading: at matched budgets, average deletion faithfulness does not separate these methods nearly as much as their folklore suggests, so the deciding factors are the task, the granularity the explanation will be read at, and cost. On cost the result is unambiguous: with near identical prediction counts SHAP ran about twice as fast overall (ratio 2.05), because its collapsed masking keeps perturbed texts short while LIME's per word markers keep them near full length. Since the methods rank words differently (Table 7) while all passing the deletion tests, deletion faithfulness at this observation count does not by itself identify a single best explanation; stronger separation would need larger samples, deeper budgets, or finer grained tests.

Limitations: one model family (frozen encoder plus MLP head), 100 documents per dataset, a whitespace word masker with ... replacement whose out of distribution effects are only partially neutralized by the shuffled controls, and wall clock timings from a shared machine.

Reproduction: notebooks 01_train (IMDB pipeline), 05_additional_datasets (Yelp, AG News), 06_benchmark (attributions, sweep, tidy results), 07_report (this document). All caches live under artifacts/; tidy results in faithfulness_results.parquet, timing in timing_results.parquet. Random seed 42 throughout. Attribution budgets: 500 and 50 evaluations per document for SHAP and LIME, occlusion at one prediction per word. Thresholds [20, 40, 60, 80], chunk sizes [1, 4, 8], combinations ['absolute_sum', 'sum_absolute', 'max_absolute']. Pairwise statistics in method_comparison.parquet.
